questions.response: write the answer and show the required work
questions.prompt: A hemisphere of radius r and a cylinder of radius r and height r with a cone removed (as shown) sit on the same plane. Use Cavalieri's principle to show that the hemisphere's volume is ⅔πr³, and conclude that a sphere has volume 4/3 πr³.
questions.prompt_markup: A hemisphere of radius r and a cylinder of radius r and height r with a cone removed (as shown) sit on the same plane. Use Cavalieri's principle to show that the hemisphere's volume is ⅔πr³, and conclude that a sphere has volume 4/3 πr³.
questions.correct_answer: Both cross-sections have area π(r² - y²), so the volumes are equal: πr³ - ⅓πr³ = ⅔πr³; the sphere is two hemispheres: 4/3 πr³.
questions.required_method: Compare the cross-section areas at height y.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: hemisphere slice radius √(r² - y²) (Pythagorean), area π(r² - y²); the other slice is a ring with outer radius r and inner radius y (the cone radius at height y), area πr² - πy²; equal areas at every height and equal heights; Cavalieri; volume cylinder minus cone = ⅔πr³; double.

questions.prompt: Let r = 6. A hemisphere of radius 6 rests on its flat base, and a cylinder of radius 6 and height 6 has a cone removed whose vertex is at the center of the bottom base and whose base is the top of the cylinder. Show that the two cross-sections have equal area at every height y (0 ≤ y ≤ 6), and use Cavalieri's principle to find the hemisphere's and the sphere's volumes.
questions.prompt_markup: Let r = 6. A hemisphere of radius 6 rests on its flat base, and a cylinder of radius 6 and height 6 has a cone removed whose vertex is at the center of the bottom base and whose base is the top of the cylinder. Show that the two cross-sections have equal area at every height y (0 ≤ y ≤ 6), and use Cavalieri's principle to find the hemisphere's and the sphere's volumes.
questions.correct_answer: Hemisphere slice π(36 - y²); ring π(36 - y²); equal at every y, equal heights, so V(hemisphere) = 216π - 72π = 144π and V(sphere) = 288π.
questions.required_method: Write both slice areas in terms of y, compare, then compute the cylinder-minus-cone volume.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: both areas as functions of y; Cavalieri's principle; 144π; doubled 288π = 4/3 π · 216.

questions.prompt: A student turns the removed cone upright (base on the bottom of the cylinder, vertex at the top) and compares the remaining solid with the hemisphere. Explain why Cavalieri's principle cannot be used for this comparison, by comparing the two cross-section areas at height y = 0.
questions.prompt_markup: A student turns the removed cone upright (base on the bottom of the cylinder, vertex at the top) and compares the remaining solid with the hemisphere. Explain why Cavalieri's principle cannot be used for this comparison, by comparing the two cross-section areas at height y = 0.
questions.correct_answer: At y = 0 the hemisphere slice has area πr², but the cylinder slice is completely removed by the cone base (area πr² - πr² = 0); the areas differ, so the principle does not apply.
questions.required_method: Compute both slice areas at y = 0.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: both areas at y = 0; unequal areas at some level; conclusion that the hypothesis of Cavalieri's principle fails.
